In writing his play, Williamson took as his inspiration Lewis’ “A Grief Observed”, which he had published under a pseudonym in 1961. Shadowlands is a play about childhood grief – Lewis’ mother died when he was eight years old – and adult grief, as we follow his slowly developing relationship with Joy, and the tragedy which we know will happen.
By turns hilarious and deeply affecting, it is a hard heart who could hear Bonneville’s final wail of grief and not want to join in.
This Shadowlands is a thoughtful revival, beautifully performed.

What initially promises to be a cursory moment shared betwixt writer and fan, quickly transforms into a meeting of minds, mutual admiration and a yearning for a more substantial friendship and even companionship. Lewis, Jeff Rawle as Major W.H. Lewis and Maggie Siff as Joy Davidman in Shadowlands at the Aldwych Theatre.
Shadowlands is a heartwrenching play that does a brilliant job of balancing warmth and humour, making a genuine emotional impact on the audience.

In his book, A Grief Observed, C.S. Lewis wrote, "The pain I feel now is the happiness I had before. That's the deal". It's that deal that William Nicholson's poignant play explores in the true story of Lewis's late-in-life love, marriage and loss. Thoughtful, tender and touching, Shadowlands examines joy and grief as a profoundly human experience.

Bonneville plays C S Lewis in William Nicholson’s play, running at the Aldwych Theatre until 9 May There’s comfort in an old-fashioned, well-made play and when Hugh Bonneville steps forward at the beginning of Shadowlands and starts to speak, there’s a sense of reassurance, of a good story about to be told.
You’ll see better acting at the Edinburgh Fringe but never mind.

cn.t: Critics find this old-fashioned tearjerker touching but creaky, praising its tender exploration of love and grief while noting its dated, starchy structure. Bonneville earns respect, though some find his performance limited.
